planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Sieglinde is an early-to-second-early German variety that bulks up quickly in cool soil.

directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart in rows 24-30 inches apart, hilling soil over the base of the stems as plants grow. Sieglinde is a long-established German heirloom producing smooth, elongated-oval tubers with pale yellow skin and pale yellow, waxy flesh that holds its shape well when boiled, making it a classic choice for potato salad across Central Europe. It bulks early relative to many other European heirloom potatoes, so plan to begin harvesting new potatoes once plants flower if a tender early crop is wanted, or leave tubers to mature fully for storage.

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Linda is a late maincrop German variety that benefits from a full season to size up smooth oval tubers.

directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart, hilling soil over the stems twice during the season to protect developing tubers from light and keep the crop evenly moist. Linda is a German heirloom known for smooth-skinned, deep yellow-fleshed tubers with a rich, dense texture well suited to roasting and mashing; it became widely known outside Germany around 2004 when lapsed EU variety registration briefly threatened its legal sale, prompting seed-saving groups to campaign for its continued availability as a garden heirloom. Allow vines to die back fully before harvesting for storage, since Linda keeps well through winter in a cool, dark location.

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost; Kipfler is a late-maturing Austrian fingerling that needs the full season to form its characteristic curved tubers.

directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep in loose, well-worked soil, since the curved fingerling tubers form best where they can expand without obstruction. Kipfler, whose name references its slender, curved shape resembling a crescent roll, produces thin-skinned, yellow-fleshed tubers with a dense, buttery, nutty flavor that holds up well to roasting whole with the skin left on. Long popular as a specialty fingerling in Austria and widely grown in Australia and New Zealand, Kipfler stores reasonably well but is often prized most for fresh eating soon after harvest.

planting.note: Plant certified seed potato pieces 4-6 weeks before last frost in light, sandy soil, which this variety's home region of Bamberg is traditionally noted for.

directions: Plant seed potato pieces 3-4 inches deep and 10-12 inches apart in light, friable soil to let the small, knobby tubers form cleanly. Bamberger Hörnla takes its name from the Franconian dialect word for 'little horn,' describing the short, curved, finger-like shape of its tubers, and traces back to the historic market-garden plots around Bamberg, Germany, a city whose old gardeners' quarter is recognized by UNESCO for its centuries of intensive vegetable cultivation. Thin-skinned with firm, waxy yellow flesh, it holds together well when boiled and is traditionally dressed simply with butter and herbs or used in regional Franconian potato salads.

common_name: Neckarkönigin Pole Bean (German Heirloom Flat Snap Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after soil has warmed and frost danger has passed; provide a tall pole or trellis, since vines climb vigorously and crop over a long season.

directions: Sow seed directly 1 inch deep at the base of poles or a trellis once soil is warm, thinning to 4-6 inches between plants. Neckarkönigin ('Queen of the Neckar,' named for the river running through the Swabian region of southwestern Germany where it was traditionally grown) is a vigorous German heirloom pole bean producing long, flat, green pods on tall climbing vines. Pick pods young and tender at 6-8 inches for the best snap-bean texture, and harvest frequently, since regular picking keeps vines setting new pods through the warm months rather than diverting energy into maturing seed.

common_name: Steirische Käferbohne (Styrian Beetle Bean, Austrian PGI Dry Bean)

planting.note: Direct sow after frost danger passes and provide sturdy poles; pods are left on the vine to dry fully rather than picked green.

directions: Sow seed directly at the base of tall poles once soil is warm, and let pods mature and dry fully on the vine rather than harvesting them green. Steirische Käferbohne is an Austrian heirloom runner bean from Styria, recognized under the European Union's Protected Geographical Indication scheme since 2011, named for the dark maroon-brown mottling on its large beige seeds that resembles a beetle's shell ('Käfer' means beetle). Grown specifically as a dry bean rather than a snap bean, it is traditionally boiled, cooled, and dressed with vinegar, onion, and Styrian pumpkin seed oil to make the classic regional dish Käferbohnensalat. Harvest whole dried pods once they rattle, then shell and finish drying the beans indoors before storage.
sources: European Commission Protected Geographical Indication register

planting.note: Start seed indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost and transplant after frost danger passes; stake or cage, since fruit grows large and heavy on indeterminate vines.

directions: Transplant into well-amended soil after hardening off, staking tall to support the heavy, pointed fruit. Ochsenherz, literally 'ox heart' in German, is a traditional German heirloom of the oxheart tomato type, bearing large, deeply lobed, heart-shaped fruit with dense, meaty flesh and a notably small seed cavity compared to round slicing tomatoes. That low-moisture, low-seed character makes it especially well suited to thick sauces and pastes that need little reduction, as well as hearty slicing for sandwiches. Water consistently through fruit set to avoid blossom end rot, since the large fruit size makes this variety more sensitive to irregular watering than smaller-fruited tomatoes.

common_name: Erfurter Mairübchen (German Heirloom Early Spring Turnip)

planting.note: Direct sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring; Mairübchen ('May turnip') is bred for fast growth to a small, tender root rather than a large storage turnip.

directions: Sow seed 1/4 inch deep directly in the garden as soon as the soil can be worked, thinning seedlings to 2-4 inches apart. Erfurter Mairübchen is a fast-maturing German heirloom turnip from Erfurt, long one of Germany's principal centers of vegetable seed growing, bred to produce small, round, white-skinned roots suited to a quick early-spring harvest rather than long storage. Pull roots while still small and young, since the mild, sweet flavor and tender texture this variety is prized for both coarsen quickly once roots size up in warming weather. Young roots are good raw, briefly braised, or added whole to spring vegetable soups along with their tender greens.
